content: The Big Mac Index is an informal metric used to measure the purchasing power parity (PPP) between two currencies. It serves as a test to determine whether market exchange rates result in goods costing the same across different countries. According to The Economist, the index aims to make exchange-rate theory more accessible and understandable. The Big Mac Index was first introduced by The Economist in September 1986 as a humorous illustration and has been published annually since then. This index also led to the coining of the term burgernomics. One proposed method for predicting exchange rate movements is based on the idea that the exchange rate between two currencies should naturally adjust so that a standard basket of goods and services costs the same in both currencies. In the context of the Big Mac Index, this basket is represented by a single Big Mac sandwich sold by McDonald's, chosen because it is produced to a consistent specification in many countries worldwide. Local McDonald's franchisees, however, have significant responsibility for negotiating input prices, which can vary. The index allows for a comparison of currencies across many countries. Some menu items are market-specific, which would complicate comparisons if used. The Big Mac PPP exchange rate between two countries is calculated by dividing the price of a Big Mac in one country (in its local currency) by the price of a Big Mac in another country (in its local currency). This calculated value is then compared to the actual exchange rate. If the calculated value is lower than the actual exchange rate, the first currency is considered undervalued relative to the second currency according to PPP theory. Conversely, if the calculated value is higher, the first currency is considered overvalued. For example, as of 2007, the U.S. dollar was undervalued by 38% relative to the British pound when comparing the price of a Big Mac in both countries. The Economist occasionally produces variations of the index. In January 2004, for instance, it introduced the Tall Latte Index, replacing the Big Mac with a cup of Starbucks coffee. Similarly, in 1997, the publication created a Coca-Cola map, which demonstrated an inverse relationship between per capita cola consumption in a country and that country's overall health. Despite its utility, the Big Mac Index has limitations in estimating PPP. In many countries, dining at international fast-food chains like McDonald's is relatively expensive compared to eating at local restaurants. Consequently, the demand for Big Macs in countries like India is not as high as in the United States. Factors such as the social status associated with eating at fast-food chains, local taxes, levels of competition, and import duties on specific items may not accurately reflect the broader economy of a country. Additionally, there is no theoretical basis for non-tradable goods and services, such as property costs, to be equal across countries. This discrepancy is one of the theoretical reasons why PPPs differ from market exchange rates over time. Nevertheless, the Big Mac Index has gained widespread recognition and is frequently cited by economists as a useful, albeit simplified, tool for understanding currency valuation and exchange rate dynamics.
